claim: Acting in the world is accompanied by a sense of agency, or experience of control over our actions and their outcomes.
source: Acting in the world is accompanied by a sense of agency, or experience of control over our actions and their outcomes.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about sense of agency that draws from established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Agency ratings, unlike confidence, were best explained by a model involving no estimates of sensory noise.
source: We compared the predictions of two computational models to participants' ratings and found that agency ratings, unlike confidence, were best explained by a model involving no estimates of sensory noise.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results comparing two models against participants' data.

claim: Agency judgments reflect first-order measures of the internal signal, without involving metacognitive computations.
source: We propose that agency judgments reflect first-order measures of the internal signal, without involving metacognitive computations, challenging the assumed link between the two cognitive processes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the computational modeling results showing the First-order model better explained the data.

claim: Agency depends on a comparison between the predicted and observed consequences of our actions, resulting in a prediction error signal if they do not match.
source: Previous research has suggested that agency depends on a comparison between the predicted and observed consequences of our actions, resulting in a prediction error signal if they do not match.
evidence: This claim is attributed to previous research and represents established theory in the field.

claim: Under the comparator model of agency, it is the prediction error signal that leads to our feeling of agency (FoA).
source: Under this widely accepted comparator model of agency, it is the prediction error signal that leads to our feeling of agency (FoA), which we assess in order to make judgments of agency (JoAs) (Carruthers, 2012; Frith et al., 2000; Haggard, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work on the comparator model.

claim: Noisy agency signals are suggested to play a role in clinical cases involving striking disruptions to agency, such as in schizophrenia.
source: Noisy agency signals are suggested to play a role in clinical cases involving striking disruptions to agency, such as in schizophrenia (Corlett et al., 2010; Fletcher and Frith, 2009; Moore and Fletcher, 2012; Robinson et al., 2016), so it is critical to understand precisely how agency signals change with uncertainty, in both healthy and clinical populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on schizophrenia and agency.

claim: Participants' feeling of agency (FoA), as measured by an implicit temporal binding effect, has been found to rely less on cues that are noisy or imprecise, and more on more informative cues.
source: In line with these models, participants' FoA, as measured by an implicit temporal binding effect, has been found to rely less on cues that are noisy or imprecise, and more on more informative cues (Moore et al., 2009; Wolpe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous empirical studies.

claim: Explicit judgments of agency (JoAs) are generally considered to be at a higher level of the processing hierarchy than feelings of agency (FoAs).
source: It is not clear that explicit JoAs incorporate noise in the same way as lower level FoAs, as JoAs are generally considered to be at a higher level of the processing hierarchy (Gallagher, 2007; Haggard and Tsakiris, 2009; Sato, 2009; Synofzik et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work on the hierarchy of agency processing.

claim: Metacognitive judgments are often operationalized as confidence ratings following discrimination responses.
source: Accordingly, metacognitive judgments are often operationalized as confidence ratings following discrimination responses (Fleming and Lau, 2014), and these second-order metacognitive ratings have been shown to monitor the uncertainty of the perceived internal signal (de Gardelle et al., 2015; Navajas et al., 2017; Rausch et al., 2017; Sanders et al., 2016; Spence et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on metacognition and confidence.

claim: Judgments of agency (JoAs) have sometimes been considered to be metacognitive reports about otherwise first-order agency signals.
source: In the literature, JoAs have sometimes been considered to be metacognitive reports about otherwise first-order agency signals (Carruthers, 2015; Metcalfe et al., 2012; Metcalfe and Greene, 2007; Miele et al., 2011; Potts and Carlson, 2019; Terhune and Hedman, 2017; Wenke et al., 2010; Zalla et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature that has conceptualized JoAs as metacognitive.

claim: Discrimination accuracy was significantly higher for low- vs. high-noise conditions.
source: In line with the intended effect of the sensory noise manipulation, accuracy was significantly higher for low- vs. high-noise conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of discrimination accuracy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was a significant interaction effect between Response Accuracy and Noise on Confidence.
source: We found a significant interaction effect between Response Accuracy and Noise on Confidence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of confidence ratings shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Sensory noise was manipulated by changing the illumination, with high sensory noise captured by low contrast, dark illumination, and low sensory noise captured by high contrast, bright illumination.
source: Sensory noise was manipulated by changing the illumination, with high sensory noise captured by low contrast, dark illumination, and low sensory noise captured by high contrast, bright illumination.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Participants first discriminated which movement they felt more agency over, and then rated their confidence in their own response.
source: Participants first discriminated which movement they felt more agency over, and then rated their confidence in their own response.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Metacognitive efficiency for each noise level was estimated using the HMetad′ toolbox.
source: M-Ratio Estimates. Metacognitive efficiency for each noise level, estimated using the HMetad′ toolbox.
evidence: This describes the analysis method used to produce the results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Accuracy was significantly lower in the high-noise compared to the low-noise condition (Mdiff = 10%, SE = 1.4%, χ2(1) = 97.60, p < 0.001, BF10 = 1.78 ✕ 1020, OR = 1.55, 95% CI [1.42, 1.70]).
source: As expected, we found a main effect of Noise, revealing significantly lower accuracy in the high-noise compared to the low-noise condition (Mdiff = 10%, SE = 1.4%, χ2(1) = 97.60, p < 0.001, BF10 = 1.78 ✕ 1020, OR = 1.55, 95% CI [1.42, 1.70]; Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the discrimination accuracy data.

claim: There was a significant interaction between Noise and Response Accuracy on confidence, F(1,8858) = 14.43, p < 0.001, BF10 = 2.19, η2p = 0.0016.
source: In line with our predictions, we found a significant interaction between Noise and Response Accuracy on confidence, F(1,8858) = 14.43, p < 0.001, BF10 = 2.19, η2p = 0.0016 (Figure 1D), with a stronger difference in confidence between correct and incorrect trials under low noise (MdiffCorrect-Incorrect = 0.58, SE = 0.044) compared to high noise (MdiffCorrect-Incorrect = 0.34, SE = 0.042).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the confidence rating data.

claim: Confidence following incorrect decisions was lower in the high-noise compared to the low-noise condition.
source: In addition to the interaction effect, we found that confidence following incorrect decisions was lower in the high-noise compared to the low-noise condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the confidence rating data.

claim: There was a significant main effect of Response on confidence, F(1,8872) = 82.64, p < 0.001, BF10 = 5.71 ✕ 1014, η2p = 0.0092.
source: Finally, we found a significant main effect of Response, F(1,8872) = 82.64, p < 0.001, BF10 = 5.71 ✕ 1014, η2p = 0.0092, with pairwise comparisons revealing significantly higher confidence ratings when participants reported feeling more agency over the stimulus in the second interval, compared to the first (Mdiff = –0.27, SE = 0.030), t(8872) = –9.09, p < 0.001.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the confidence rating data.

claim: Participants' metacognitive efficiency (M-Ratio) was above-chance in both conditions.
source: In order to further ensure that participants' confidence ratings reflected metacognitive processing, especially given relatively low accuracy under high noise, we checked that their metacognitive efficiency (M-Ratio) was above-chance in both conditions (Figure 1E; see Appendix 3 for full analysis).
evidence: This claim is supported by the M-Ratio analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There was a significant interaction effect between Noise and Delay on JoA, F(1,52) = 61.16, p < 0.001, BF10 = 3.78 ✕ 106, η2p = 0.54, 95% CI [0.35, 0.67].
source: We found a significant interaction effect between Noise and Delay, F(1,52) = 61.16, p < 0.001, BF10 = 3.78 ✕ 106, η2p = 0.54, 95% CI [0.35, 0.67], with a less extreme negative slope across delay values in the high-noise condition (βHigh = -5.93, SE = 0.69), compared to low-noise (βLow = -9.84, SE = 0.77) (Figure 2C), suggesting that JoAs met our first criterion.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the agency rating data.

claim: There was a significant main effect of Delay on JoA, F(1,39) = 132.05, p < 0.001, BF10 = 14486.52, η2p = 0.77, 95% CI [0.64, 0.85].
source: We also found a significant main effect of Delay, F(1,39) = 132.05, p < 0.001, BF10 = 14486.52, η2p = 0.77, 95% CI [0.64, 0.85], replicating previous findings that showed increasing delays of the virtual hand movement to lead to lower JoAs (Krugwasser et al., 2019; Stern et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the agency rating data and citations to previous findings.

claim: The majority of participants (37 out of 40) showed the effect of JoAs decreasing with delay in both conditions.
source: We found this effect of JoAs decreasing with delay for the majority of participants (37 out of 40) included in this analysis in both conditions, indicating that participants were able to make meaningful ratings, even in the high-noise condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of individual participant data.

claim: The First-order model could better explain the JoA data than the Second-order model at the group level (ΔBICSecond-First = 2728).
source: Against the notion that agency ratings and confidence arise from analogous uncertainty monitoring computations, the group-level analysis revealed that the First-order model could better explain the JoA data (ΔBICSecond-First = 2728, Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the BIC comparison of computational models shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The First-order model could better explain the data for 38 out of 40 participants, whereas the Second-order model provided a better fit for only 2.
source: Fitting the two models to each participant revealed results consistent with the group-level analysis: The First-order model could better explain the data for 38 out of 40 participants, whereas the Second-order model provided a better fit for only 2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the subject-wise BIC comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The protected exceedance probabilities (PEPs) indicated that the First-order model occurs most frequently in the population for agency ratings.
source: Also in line with this, the PEPs indicated that the First-order model occurs most frequently in the population (Figure 4D), with the predicted frequencies shown in Figure 4E.
evidence: This claim is supported by the PEP analysis shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: The Second-order model could better explain confidence ratings than the First-order model (ΔBICFirst-Second = 1121).
source: As expected, the Second-order model could better explain confidence ratings (ΔBICFirst-Second = 1121, Figure 5A), suggesting confidence to involve metacognitive computations, in contrast to JoAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the BIC comparison of computational models for confidence ratings shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The PEPs suggested the Second-order model to be the most frequently occurring model in the population for confidence ratings.
source: The PEPs also suggested the Second-order model to be the most frequently occurring model in the population (Figure 5C), with estimated frequencies shown in Figure 5D.
evidence: This claim is supported by the PEP analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: The Second-order model provided a better fit for confidence ratings in 24 out of 40 participants, the First-order model provided a better fit in 13, and a BIC difference of less than 2 in 3.
source: The subject-wise BIC comparison revealed the Second-order model to provide a better fit in 24 out of 40 participants, the First-order model to provide a better fit in 13, and a BIC difference of less than 2 (suggesting neither model being a conclusively better fit) in 3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the subject-wise BIC comparison shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Uncertainty did not affect agency ratings in the same way as it does confidence ratings.
source: Here, we tested whether JoAs are metacognitive in a computational sense by examining whether they involve the same second-order uncertainty monitoring computations as metacognitive confidence ratings, or whether they can only be said to be metacognitive at a broad conceptual level. We found that uncertainty did not affect agency ratings in the same way as it does confidence ratings, suggesting that any effect of noise is better considered as an influence on first-order signals, without involving metacognitive noise estimates.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the computational modeling results comparing agency and confidence ratings.

claim: Participants can make metacognitive confidence judgments about agency decisions.
source: Importantly, we also found that participants can make metacognitive confidence judgments about agency decisions, but that subjective agency ratings do not share these computations, despite the same basic agency task and noise manipulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of the confidence task showing above-chance metacognitive efficiency.

claim: Confidence judgments about agency should be considered as the metacognitive level of an agency processing hierarchy, with agency judgments as explicit first-order judgments.
source: We suggest that confidence judgments about agency should be considered as the metacognitive level of an agency processing hierarchy, with agency judgments as explicit first-order judgments.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal inferred from the experimental results.

claim: The dependence of agency ratings on the noise condition may be highly relevant both for future experimental design and in the interpretation of explicit agency reports.
source: Although we suggest that JoAs do not imply metacognitive uncertainty monitoring, the dependence of agency ratings on the noise condition should not be overlooked and may be highly relevant both for future experimental design and in the interpretation of explicit agency reports.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications of the findings for future research.

claim: The findings are in line with multifactorial accounts of JoAs as involving a variety of both internal and external cues.
source: This finding is in line with multifactorial accounts of JoAs as involving a variety of both internal and external cues (Synofzik et al., 2008), and with the expanding empirical work investigating a range of contextual effects on agency (Minohara et al., 2016; Wen, 2019).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous theoretical and empirical work through citations.

claim: The findings fit within cue integration theories of agency, with the delay information being weighted less heavily when the signal is made less precise.
source: Our work also fits within cue integration theories of agency (Moore and Fletcher, 2012; Synofzik et al., 2013), with the delay information being weighted less heavily when the signal is made less precise.
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to cue integration theories through citations and inference.

claim: Having a perceivable manipulation such as reduced visibility in order to add noise to feedback cues may itself act as an additional factor influencing agency judgments.
source: Further, these results are relevant to empirical work examining cue integration in agency, as they suggest that having a perceivable manipulation such as reduced visibility in order to add noise to feedback cues may itself act as an additional factor influencing agency judgments, which should be accounted for in design and analysis.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for experimental design.

claim: The findings support the suggestions of previous work that, while Bayesian confidence computations may underlie pre-reflective FoA, explicit JoAs reflect a different computational mechanism, and factor in different contextual information.
source: Our findings support the suggestions of previous work that, while Bayesian confidence computations may underlie pre-reflective FoA, explicit JoAs reflect a different computational mechanism, and factor in different contextual information (Legaspi and Toyoizumi, 2019; Wen, 2019).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous work through citations.

claim: Sensory noise information may influence lower level, perceptual agency signals by making them more variable, and these more variable signals then feed into higher level JoAs, but estimates of the noise do not contribute as an additional cue to inform the JoAs.
source: Taken into the context of two-step models of agency (Synofzik et al., 2008), our results suggest that sensory noise information may influence lower level, perceptual agency signals by making them more variable, and that these more variable signals then feed into higher level JoAs, but that estimates of the noise do not contribute as an additional cue to inform the JoAs.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of agency processing based on the experimental results.

claim: Higher order agency states remain naive with regard to how noisy the lower level signals are.
source: Hence, higher order agency states remain naive with regard to how noisy the lower level signals are.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that JoAs do not involve metacognitive noise estimates.

claim: If explicit JoAs do not consider uncertainty, this could lead to extreme agency reports despite unreliable evidence and inaccurate agency inferences in clinical cases.
source: If explicit JoAs do not consider this uncertainty (as our findings indicate), this could lead to extreme agency reports despite unreliable evidence and inaccurate agency inferences.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications of the findings for clinical populations.

claim: The findings are in line with work on agency misattributions in schizophrenia suggesting that they may be due to particularly noisy low level agency information, possibly due to dysregulated neurotransmitter activity.
source: This is in line with work on agency misattributions in schizophrenia suggesting that they may be due to particularly noisy low level agency information, possibly due to dysregulated neurotransmitter activity (Corlett et al., 2010; Fletcher and Frith, 2009; Moore and Fletcher, 2012; Robinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous work on schizophrenia through citations.

claim: The confidence task served as a positive control task to ensure that the noise manipulation had the expected effect on a metacognitive judgment.
source: Importantly, we note that the findings that we describe here do not rely on a comparison between tasks. The confidence task merely served as a positive control task to ensure that our noise manipulation had the expected effect on a metacognitive judgment and that the second-order model we built best predicted the results of computations we knew to be higher-order.
evidence: This describes the methodological role of the confidence task in the study design.

claim: The conclusions about the computations underlying the JoAs are limited by the manipulations used in the task.
source: Our conclusions about the computations underlying the JoAs are limited by the manipulations used in the task.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study.

claim: Noise was manipulated externally, not directly internally, and only added noise to the perceived delay signals, rather than motor or somatosensory cues.
source: First, we manipulated noise externally, not directly internally, and only added noise to the perceived delay signals, rather than motor or somatosensory cues.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental manipulation.

claim: Action selection noise was not manipulated, which has been shown to influence agency independently of the comparator signal.
source: We additionally did not manipulate action selection noise, which has been shown to influence agency independently of the comparator signal (Wenke et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental manipulation with a citation to previous work.

claim: It is unclear whether the findings apply to other kinds of agency manipulations beyond altering the timing of the action outcome.
source: Further, our conclusions hold for the agency manipulation we used, namely altering the timing of the action outcome. But, it is unclear whether these findings apply to other kinds of agency manipulations.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study regarding generalizability.

claim: The approach of introducing delay in the visual feedback has been validated against other measures of agency in previous work using the virtual hand agency paradigm.
source: Previous work using this virtual hand agency paradigm has also validated the approach of introducing delay in the visual feedback against other measures of agency (Krugwasser et al., 2019; Stern et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous validation studies.

claim: The results should be considered in the context of the particular agency rating scale used, as this will constrain participants' rating behavior.
source: Our results should also be considered in the context of the particular agency rating scale we used, as this will constrain participants' rating behavior.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation regarding the rating scale.

claim: Similar agency scales are commonly used in agency research.
source: Similar agency scales are commonly used in agency research (Dewey and Knoblich, 2014; Imaizumi and Tanno, 2019; Kawabe et al., 2013; Metcalfe and Greene, 2007; Miele et al., 2011; Sato and Yasuda, 2005; Stern et al., 2020; Voss et al., 2017; Wen et al., 2015a), so the results presented here are relevant to understand the computations of agency ratings discussed in the existing literature.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies using similar scales.

claim: A 2IFC task on agency followed by a confidence judgment may be more adequate to measure a metacognitive component of agency processing.
source: Thus, our results suggest that the JoAs measured in the literature do not indicate metacognitive computations. On the basis of these results, we concur with recent work (Wang et al., 2020) that suggests that a 2IFC task on agency followed by a confidence judgment may be more adequate to measure a metacognitive component of agency processing.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the findings, with a citation to previous work.

claim: The experiment was pre-registered (osf.io/pyjhm).
source: The experiment was pre-registered (osf.io/pyjhm), and we describe deviations from the pre-registered plan.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological transparency of the study.

claim: A sample size of 32 participants was pre-registered based on power estimates from similar tasks.
source: We pre-registered a sample size of 32 participants (based on power estimates from similar tasks).
evidence: This describes the pre-registered sample size and its justification.

claim: Data was collected until 40 participants that displayed the basic and expected manipulation effect of illumination were reached.
source: We collected data until we reached 40 participants that displayed the basic and expected manipulation effect of illumination (see above).
evidence: This describes the actual data collection procedure.

claim: 47 young, healthy participants between 18 and 35 years of age (M = 27.15, SD = 4.68) were tested in Berlin.
source: We tested 47 young, healthy participants between 18 and 35 years of age (M = 27.15, SD = 4.68) in Berlin.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: Participants were required to be right handed (Edinburgh Handedness Inventory score: M = 79.5, SD = 23.6).
source: To participate in the study, we required that participants were right handed (Edinburgh Handedness Inventory score: M = 79.5, SD = 23.6), had no injury or condition preventing or restricting movement of the right index finger, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and were fluent in English.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: The ethics committee of the Institute of Psychology at the Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin approved the study (Nr. 2020–29), which conformed to the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: The ethics committee of the Institute of Psychology at the Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin approved the study (Nr. 2020–29), which conformed to the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a statement about the ethical approval of the study.

claim: A LEAP Motion controller was used to track participants' hand motion and to control in real time the movement of a virtual hand displayed on the screen.
source: We used a LEAP Motion controller (Leap Motion Inc, San Francisco, CA) to track participants' hand motion and to control in real time the movement of a virtual hand displayed on the screen.
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus.

claim: The experiment ran on a Dell Latitude 5591 laptop with a display resolution of 1920 × 1080 (refresh rate = 60 Hz) using software built in Unity 5.6.1.
source: The experiment ran on a Dell Latitude 5591 laptop (Intel core i5 with 16 GB of RAM) with a display resolution of 1920 × 1080 (refresh rate = 60 Hz) using software built in Unity 5.6.1, and was modified from software used in previous studies (Krugwasser et al., 2019; Stern et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus and software.

claim: Blackout curtains were used during all testing to keep the lighting conditions within the room as consistent as possible.
source: Blackout curtains were used during all testing to keep the lighting conditions within the room as consistent as possible.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail to control environmental conditions.

claim: Each participant completed two tasks: a confidence-rating task and an agency-rating task.
source: Each participant completed two tasks: a confidence-rating task (Figure 1B) and an agency-rating task (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: In both tasks, sensory noise was manipulated orthogonally to the decision variable by controlling the visibility of the virtual hand.
source: In both tasks, we manipulated sensory uncertainty by controlling the visibility of the virtual hand, which is computationally analogous to adding noise to the signal. This allowed us to compare the effect of noise on JoAs and confidence. Importantly, we manipulated sensory noise orthogonally to the decision variable, as done by previous work (Bang and Fleming, 2018; de Gardelle et al., 2015; Spence et al., 2016), which allowed us to precisely examine effects of noise without altering the true degree of control that the participants had over the virtual hand movement.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation and its justification with citations.

claim: A short thresholding procedure was done prior to starting the experiment to set the illumination level that would be used in the high-noise condition of the main tasks.
source: Prior to starting the experiment, participants completed the Edinburgh handedness scale. We then did a short thresholding procedure to set the illumination level that would be used in the high-noise condition of the main tasks.
evidence: This describes a methodological procedure.

claim: The baseline illumination levels were set in the Unity environment with a directional light intensity of 0 in the high-noise condition and 0.001 in the low-noise condition.
source: The baseline illumination levels were set in the Unity environment with a directional light intensity of 0 in the high-noise condition and 0.001 in the low-noise condition, but the brightness of the screen was then further thresholded in order to account for differences in eyesight and lighting conditions in the room.
evidence: This describes the specific parameter settings for the noise manipulation.

claim: All participants performed the agency-rating task first so that subjective ratings would not be biased by the structure or ratings of the confidence task.
source: All participants performed the agency-rating task first so that subjective ratings would not be biased by the structure or ratings of the confidence task.
evidence: This describes the task order and its justification.

claim: After every movement in the agency-rating task, participants rated their agency on a scale from 1 to 6.
source: After every movement, participants rated their agency on a scale from 1 to 6 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the response measure in the agency-rating task.

claim: Participants were explained that the term 'agency' referred to how much control they had over the movement of the virtual hand, and they were asked to focus specifically on the timing of the movement.
source: We explained that the term 'agency' referred to how much control they had over the movement of the virtual hand, and they were asked to focus specifically on the timing of the movement.
evidence: This describes the instructions given to participants.

claim: Overall, 2.4% of trials were marked as errors in the confidence task, and 1.9% were marked as errors in the agency rating task.
source: Overall, 2.4% of trials were marked as errors in the confidence task, and 1.9% were marked as errors in the agency rating task.
evidence: This describes the error rate in the tasks.

claim: There were 60 trials per delay level and lighting condition in the agency-rating task, for a total of 480 trials, split across six blocks.
source: There were 60 trials per delay level and lighting condition, for a total of 480 trials, split across six blocks.
evidence: This describes the number of trials in the agency-rating task.

claim: The agency-rating task took approximately 45 min.
source: The agency-rating task took approximately 45 min.
evidence: This describes the duration of the agency-rating task.

claim: In the confidence-rating task, participants made two consecutive movements, decided which virtual hand movement they had more agency over, and rated their confidence in their response from 1 to 6.
source: Participants again flexed and extended their right index finger under the LEAP motion tracker, while looking at the virtual hand on the screen. In contrast to the agency-rating task, they made two consecutive movements, each cued by the appearance of the virtual hand, and separated with a blank gray screen. They then decided which virtual hand movement they had more agency over, and rated their confidence in their response from 1 (lowest) to 6 (highest).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for the confidence-rating task.

claim: The difference in delay levels between the movements in each trial of the confidence task was staircased using an online 2-down-1-up staircasing procedure aiming to achieve an overall accuracy of approximately 71%.
source: The difference in delay levels between the movements in each trial was staircased, with one of the two movements always having no delay and the other being adjusted according to an online 2-down-1-up staircasing procedure aiming to achieve an overall accuracy of approximately 71%.
evidence: This describes the adaptive procedure used in the confidence task.

claim: There were 100 trials per noise condition in the confidence task, for a total of 200 trials across five blocks.
source: There were 100 trials per noise condition, for a total of 200 trials across five blocks.
evidence: This describes the number of trials in the confidence task.

claim: The confidence task took approximately 45 min.
source: The confidence task took approximately 45 min.
evidence: This describes the duration of the confidence task.

claim: Any participants for whom discrimination accuracy in the high-noise condition was not lower than in the low-noise condition in the confidence task were excluded from the analyses of the agency rating task.
source: We therefore excluded from the following analyses any participants for whom discrimination accuracy in the high-noise condition was not lower than in the low-noise condition in the confidence task.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion for the analysis.

claim: All the results remain largely the same, and the conclusions unchanged, when data from all participants are included in the analyses.
source: We note that all the results described below remain largely the same, and the conclusions unchanged, when we include the data from all participants in the analyses (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This describes a robustness check of the results.

claim: Linear mixed-effects models were built using the 'lme4' package in R.
source: We tested our main hypotheses using the 'lme4' package (Bates et al., 2015) in R (R Development Core Team, 2020) to build linear mixed-effects models.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis software used.

claim: All hypotheses were tested using two-tailed tests and an alpha level of 0.05, and additionally using Bayes factors.
source: All hypotheses were tested using two-tailed tests and an alpha level of 0.05, and additionally using Bayes factors, which we computed with the 'BayesTestR' package (Makowski et al., 2019) using default priors.
evidence: This describes the statistical testing approach.

claim: Metacognitive efficiency (M-Ratio) was measured using the HMeta-d′ toolbox.
source: To analyse metacognitive ability from the confidence task, we measured metacognitive efficiency (M-Ratio) using the HMeta-d′ toolbox (Fleming, 2017).
evidence: This describes the method used to measure metacognitive efficiency.

claim: A model recovery analysis was performed across the set of winning parameter values of each model across participants, confirming that the models were distinguishable from one another over the entire relevant parameter space.
source: We also performed a model recovery analysis across the set of winning parameter values of each model across participants, confirming that the models were distinguishable from one another over the entire relevant parameter space (see Appendix 4).
evidence: This describes a validation procedure for the computational models.

claim: The Second-order model assumed that agency ratings behave like confidence as described by Bayesian-confidence models, namely as the posterior probability that a decision is correct, given the strength of the internal evidence and the decision.
source: The Second-order model assumed that agency ratings behave like confidence as described by Bayesian-confidence models, namely as the posterior probability that a decision is correct, given the strength of the internal evidence and the decision (Navajas et al., 2017; Sanders et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the theoretical basis of the Second-order model with citations.

claim: In the Second-order model, the computation of the posterior probability requires the observer to have second-order access to estimate their own sensory noise.
